back: F = q[E(r) + v x B(r)], the sum of an electric part qE and a magnetic part q(v x B). The magnetic part is perpendicular to v, does no work, and leaves the speed unchanged.

1 T is the field in which a unit charge (1 C) moving perpendicular to B at 1 m/s feels a force of 1 N. [B] = [F/qv], so 1 T = 1 N s C^-1 m^-1. One gauss = 10^-4 T; the earth's field is about 3.6 x 10^-5 T.

front: When is the magnetic force zero?
back: When the charge is at rest (v = 0), or when v is parallel or antiparallel to B (sin theta = 0). Otherwise F = qvB sin theta, perpendicular to both v and B.

F = I l x B, with |l| equal to the length of the rod and its direction the direction of the current. The current I itself is not a vector, and B here is the external field. For a bent wire, F = sum of I dl x B.
r = mv/qB, from mv^2/r = qvB. Larger momentum gives a larger circle; a stronger field bends the path more tightly. The magnetic force does no work, so the speed is constant.

omega = 2 pi nu = qB/m, so nu = qB/2 pi m. It contains neither v nor r, so every revolution takes the same time T = 2 pi m/qB however large the orbit grows. This is the working principle of the cyclotron.
p = v_parallel T = 2 pi m v_parallel/qB. The parallel component of velocity is untouched by the field and carries the particle along the axis; the perpendicular component supplies the circle.

Two dees in a uniform field with an alternating voltage across the gap at nu_c = qB/2 pi m. The particle crosses the gap twice per turn, gaining qV each time. Maximum energy at radius R: K = q^2 B^2 R^2 / 2m. Relativistic mass increase limits it to modest energies.
Crossed E and B fields balance when qE = qvB, so only charges with v = E/B pass undeviated. The charge cancels, so the selected speed is independent of mass and of the sign of the charge.
dB = (mu_0/4 pi) I (dl x r)/r^3, magnitude dB = (mu_0/4 pi) I dl sin(theta)/r^2. The field is perpendicular to the plane of dl and r, and zero along the line of dl.
mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1, so mu_0/4 pi = 10^-7 T m A^-1. It is linked to the permittivity by mu_0 epsilon_0 = 1/c^2; fixing either constant fixes the other.

front: Field on the axis of a circular loop
back: B = mu_0 I R^2 / 2(x^2 + R^2)^(3/2), along the axis, with N turns giving an extra factor N. At the centre (x = 0) this reduces to B = mu_0 N I/2R, e.g. 6.28 x 10^-4 T for 100 turns, R = 10 cm, I = 1 A.

oint B.dl = mu_0 I over the closed boundary of a surface, I being the total current through the surface. Simplified form when B is tangential and constant: BL = mu_0 I_e. Sign of I from the right-hand rule.

front: Field of a long straight wire
back: B = mu_0 I/2 pi r, tangential to circles concentric with the wire. The field has cylindrical symmetry, is finite at any non-zero distance, and grows without limit only as r approaches zero. Right-hand rule: thumb along current, fingers curl along B.
For r < a only the fraction r^2/a^2 of the current is enclosed, so B = mu_0 I r/2 pi a^2 - proportional to r. For r > a, B = mu_0 I/2 pi r. The field is maximum at the surface, B = mu_0 I/2 pi a.
B = mu_0 n I, where n is the number of turns per unit length. Uniform and parallel to the axis inside, essentially zero outside. Length must be much greater than the radius for this to hold.

B = mu_0 N I/2 pi r = mu_0 n I inside the winding, and B = 0 in the hole and outside it, since an outside amperian loop encloses no net current. Used where the field must be confined; slightly non-uniform across the cross-section.
f = mu_0 I1 I2/2 pi d per unit length. Parallel currents attract, antiparallel currents repel - the opposite of the rule for charges. F_ba = -F_ab, consistent with Newton's third law.

The steady current which, in each of two very long parallel conductors one metre apart in vacuum, produces a force of 2 x 10^-7 N per metre. Adopted in 1946. One coulomb is the charge crossing a section in 1 s at 1 A.
In a field lying in the plane of the loop, tau = I A B. In general tau = I A B sin theta, where theta is the angle between the normal to the loop and B. The net force is zero in a uniform field.
m = N I A, directed by the right-hand thumb rule. Unit A m^2. The torque is tau = m x B, analogous to tau = p x E for an electric dipole.

m parallel to B is stable: the torque vanishes and small rotations are restored. m antiparallel to B is unstable: the torque grows with the rotation. This is why a compass needle settles along the field.

For x >> R, B = (mu_0/4 pi)(2m/x^3) on the axis and (mu_0/4 pi)(m/x^3) in the plane of the loop. Replacing mu_0 by 1/epsilon_0 and m by p gives the electric dipole field. Ampere proposed that all magnetism is due to circulating currents.

A many-turn coil in a radial field feels tau = NIAB (sin theta = 1 by design). A spring balances it, k phi = NIAB, so phi = (NAB/k) I: deflection proportional to current. The soft iron core makes the field radial and stronger.
Current sensitivity phi/I = NAB/k; voltage sensitivity phi/V = NAB/kR. Doubling N doubles the first but also doubles R, leaving the second unchanged - so ammeter and voltmeter conversions differ.

Ammeter: a small shunt resistance in parallel with the coil, so most of the current bypasses it and the instrument resistance is small - the galvanometer is far too sensitive and too resistive to use directly in series. Voltmeter: a large resistance in series, connected in parallel with the section, so it draws very little current.
